lesson.subtitle: Lesson 23 -- The Follow-up That Works
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávio Masaharu Kuroda | Lesson 23 -- The Follow-up That Works
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect in follow-ups (I haven't heard back, have you had a chance, has anything changed)

listenings.text: Most deals do not die with a no. They die with silence. And most salespeople make the same two mistakes when a customer goes quiet. The first mistake is guilt: they write, I haven't heard from you, as if the customer did something wrong. The second mistake is the empty nudge: just checking in, with nothing new to say. A follow-up that works always brings something. A new number, a short summary, a question about what has changed. Customers rarely go quiet because of you. Usually their priorities have changed, or their budget has moved. So ask about that. And give yourself a limit. After four messages with no answer, send a short breakup email. You will be surprised how many people answer that one.

I go quiet on suppliers more often than I like to admit. It is almost never about the supplier. Last month, for example, our CEO changed the priorities for the quarter, and three projects went on hold in one afternoon. I had four suppliers waiting for an answer, and I simply had nothing to tell them. The emails I answered were the short ones. One supplier wrote: I know things have probably changed on your side. Has the project moved, or is it only the timing? I could answer that in one line. The emails I didn't answer were the long ones, with a new presentation attached. And the one I remember asked me to circle back in January, and then really called me on the second of January.
